title: Nesting Gift Boxes
story: A gift shop packs fragile orders in nested pouches, boxes and crates. The packer logs every move with one character: ( opens a pouch and ) closes it, [ and ] do the same for a box, { and } for a crate.
A log is fine only if the packer always closed the container they were working in: you cannot seal a crate while a box inside it is open. A script checks each log before the order ships.
task: Write packedRight(log). Return true if every container is closed by the matching kind, in the right order, with nothing left open. Otherwise return false.

A close is correct only if it matches the most recently opened container still open. Any kind may sit inside any other (a crate inside a pouch is fine); only the order of opening and closing matters. An empty log is fine: return true.

examples.explanation: Open crate, box, pouch; then close pouch, box, crate. Each close matches the newest container still open.
The packer opens a crate, then a box, then closes the crate while the box is still open. Each container opens and closes once, so a count looks fine, but the order is wrong.
The box opens and closes. Then two pouches open and only one closes, leaving a pouch open.

hints: In {[()]}, when the packer types ), which container must it close: the first opened, or the last?
A close always refers to the newest container still open. Once closed, the one before it is the newest open again. That is last in, first out.
Counting is not enough: ([)] has one of each kind but is wrong. You must remember the order the open containers were opened in.
Keep a stack of open containers. On an opener, push it. On a closer, the stack must be non-empty and its top must be the matching opener; pop it. At the end, the stack must be empty.
bruteForce: Repeatedly delete any adjacent matching pair, (), [] or {}, until none is left. If the string ends up empty, the log was fine.
Each pass scans the whole string and may remove only one pair: a 10,000-character log can need 5,000 passes, tens of millions of steps. A stack does it in one pass.

walkthrough: Every close must match the newest container still open. A stack gives you exactly "newest first": push on open, check the top on close.
• {, [, (: push all three. Stack: { [ (, with ( on top.
• ): the top is (, a match. Pop. Stack: { [.
• ]: the top is [, a match. Pop. Stack: {.
• }: the top is {, a match. Pop. The stack is empty at the end, so return true.
In {[}], after {[ the top is [ but the next character is }: no match, so return false at once.
Two checks are easy to forget: a close on an empty stack (] alone), and openers left on the stack at the end ((().
solution.timeWhy: One pass, and each push or pop is O(1).
solution.spaceWhy: A log of only openings puts every character on the stack.
solution.takeaway: When the most recent unfinished thing must be finished first, use a stack. The same pattern checks nested HTML tags, matching keywords in code, and undo histories.
